reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A mechanical complication after gastrojejunostomy (classically Billroth II reconstruction) in which the afferent biliopancreatic limb becomes obstructed
Acute obstruction is a surgical emergency and can lead to duodenal stump blowout, pancreatitis, or ischaemia
Chronic partial obstruction causes postprandial right upper quadrant pain relieved by bilious vomiting that characteristically contains little or no food
Stasis in the loop predisposes to bacterial overgrowth with malabsorption, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and vitamin B12 deficiency
Cross-sectional imaging shows a dilated, fluid-filled afferent limb, sometimes with a U-shaped configuration
Definitive management of significant obstruction is surgical revision, with endoscopic or drainage measures in selected cases
The syndrome should be considered in any patient with prior gastric surgery presenting with bilious vomiting and upper abdominal pain
reference.pathophysiology: Afferent loop syndrome develops when the afferent (biliopancreatic) limb of a gastrojejunostomy becomes obstructed by kinking, adhesions, internal herniation, stenosis, recurrent tumour, or a long redundant loop. Bile and pancreatic secretions accumulate in the closed or partially obstructed limb, raising intraluminal pressure; once the pressure overcomes the obstruction the accumulated fluid is discharged suddenly, producing projectile bilious vomiting and relief of pain. Chronic stasis fosters small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth, deconjugation of bile salts, and consequent fat and vitamin malabsorption, while acute complete obstruction risks duodenal stump rupture and pancreatitis.
additionalDifferentials: Gastric outlet obstruction from other causes
Recurrent or new malignancy at the anastomosis
additionalInvestigations: CT of the abdomen showing a dilated fluid-filled afferent limb
Upper endoscopy to assess the anastomosis and exclude recurrent tumour
Hepatobiliary imaging where biliary obstruction is suspected
Serum amylase/lipase and liver function tests
Breath testing or clinical assessment for bacterial overgrowth and nutritional deficiencies
redFlags: Severe pain with signs of duodenal stump rupture or peritonitis
Sepsis or haemodynamic instability suggesting closed-loop obstruction or ischaemia
Weight loss and a mass suggesting recurrent malignancy
reference.prognosis: Acute afferent loop obstruction carries significant risk and requires urgent intervention, whereas chronic partial obstruction can often be corrected surgically with good functional outcomes; untreated stasis leads to progressive malabsorption.
pitfalls: Attributing bilious vomiting after gastric surgery to benign causes and missing obstruction
Overlooking bacterial overgrowth and consequent B12 and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
Delaying surgery in acute obstruction, risking duodenal stump blowout
Failing to exclude recurrent malignancy as the cause of the obstruction
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Refer acute obstruction for emergency surgical decompression to prevent duodenal stump blowout, pancreatitis and ischaemia
Correct significant chronic obstruction with surgical revision of the anastomosis, typically conversion to a Roux-en-Y configuration that drains the biliopancreatic limb
Consider endoscopic or percutaneous decompression and stenting in selected patients unfit for surgery or with malignant obstruction
Treat small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth with rotating antibiotics to relieve malabsorption
Replace vitamin B12 and fat-soluble vitamins and provide nutritional support for malabsorption
Investigate for and manage recurrent tumour at the anastomosis as a cause of obstruction
Provide fluid resuscitation, analgesia and nasogastric decompression as supportive measures in acute presentations
